article.body_html:
A monthly rental on a steady salary is simple: one payment, one receipt. With irregular income the question changes. Paying a month at once means a large sum leaves your account before you have earned the next one, while smaller payments need a reminder, a cut-off day and a receipt every time. No payment schedule for Thuê xe máy Nguyễn Hà has been confirmed, so the sensible approach is to ask which schedules the shop accepts, choose the one that fits your income and agree the receipts before the first payment.

Three ways to pay for a month

ScheduleWhat it offersWhat to ask the shop
All at the startOne receipt and no payment dates to remember, but the largest outlay on day oneWhat exactly the payment covers, and what happens to the unused part if you return the bike early
Week by weekSmaller sums that can follow your income, but a payment due every seven daysWhich day is the cut-off, whether a late payment has a grace period, and whether the instalments keep the monthly rate
A fixed date each monthOne payment on a day that matches when you are paidWhich date, what happens if it falls outside the shop's opening hours, and who confirms receipt

A shop may accept one schedule and not another, and nothing here says that Thuê xe máy Nguyễn Hà accepts any of them. Ask first.

Weekly payments are not the same as weekly rentals

Paying a monthly rental in weekly parts and renting by the week are two different arrangements, and the price can differ between them. The shop's reference prices for a manual bike are 700,000 to 800,000 VND for a week and 1,000,000 to 1,200,000 VND for a month. For illustration, four weekly rentals at the weekly reference price would come to 2,800,000 to 3,200,000 VND, far more than the monthly reference price. A monthly rental paid in four equal parts is a different thing: each part would be a quarter of the monthly price. Which of the two you are agreeing to has to be said in words, and the real prices are the ones the shop confirms when you book.

What each payment should leave you holding

  • The amount and the date it was paid.
  • The period it covers, written as start and end dates rather than "one week".
  • The bike, identified by its plate number.
  • Who received it, and by what method: cash or, if the shop accepts one, a bank transfer to a named account. For a transfer, confirm the payee before you send anything.
  • The next due date and what happens if you pay late.

A photo of each receipt, kept in a folder with the booking record, makes any later disagreement easier to settle.

Choosing a schedule when income is uneven

  1. Start from your own calendar, not the shop's. List the dates on which money reaches you and the gaps between them.
  2. Pick the schedule whose due dates fall just after those dates, so that no payment is due while you are waiting to be paid.
  3. Keep a buffer. Set aside the cost of one extra payment, so that a late invoice does not become a late rental payment.
  4. Agree the cut-off in writing. A due date with no stated consequence is easy to misread in both directions.
  5. Tell the shop before a payment will be late. A message sent in advance gives the shop a chance to answer; silence does not.

If no schedule the shop accepts fits your income, it may be worth asking about a shorter booking or a different bike type, rather than agreeing to dates you cannot keep. The page of daily, weekly and monthly rates shows how the shop describes its price ranges.

Before the first payment

Write down the schedule you want, the receipts you expect and the questions above in one message, and send it before you pay anything. Store the reply with the photos of the bike taken at handover. If you want the shop's own monthly rates, its page on monthly rentals lists them with booking details. Questions about payment dates can go to the shop by phone on 0334 699 969, between 09:00 and 21:00 daily.
